data.name: Review1Text
data.value: We saw the aurora on the very first night! The guide knew spots without tourists and told stories that gave us chills. Best trip in years.

data.name: Review2Text
data.value: Dragon Eggs, a storm on the Barents Sea and fresh cod soup. Flawless logistics: picked up in Murmansk, back in time for the train.

data.name: Review3Text
data.value: I dreamed of seeing the northern lights — and saw them over the ocean. The driver met me at the airport, everything went calmly and on schedule.

data.name: Review4Text
data.value: We went in March with the whole family. The kids still talk about the Dragon Eggs and the cod soup. Organisation gets a five.

data.name: Review5Text
data.value: We caught the aurora on the second try: the guide honestly warned about clouds and moved the trip. I respect that. One star off for the long drive — but the North was worth it.

data.name: Review6Text
data.value: I came for the aurora — and got it the very first evening, right over the ocean. The guides speak English, everything was easy.

data.name: Review7Text
data.value: Batareysky waterfall in a storm was the strongest impression of my year. Between the stops we were saved by the warm minivan and hot tea.

data.name: Review8Text
data.value: Booked the tour for my wife's birthday. The team arranged a surprise cake at the edge of the world — unforgettable.

data.name: Review9Text
data.value: A dream came true — standing on the shore of the Arctic Ocean. It was very handy that I could book on the site in Chinese.

data.name: Place1Detail1
data.value: Huge, perfectly rounded boulders cover the shore of the Barents Sea. Waves have been polishing them for thousands of years, and the beach now looks as if a dragon left its clutch here. The stones are most dramatic in a storm, when the ocean rolls them with a deep rumble.

data.name: Place1Detail2
data.value: The beach lies beyond the village, on the way to Batareysky waterfall. Walk carefully: the stones get slippery in the rain. The best light for photos is the polar sunset, when the low sun paints the boulders in warm gold.

data.name: Place2Detail1
data.value: At low tide the ribs of early 20th-century wooden fishing ships rise out of the bay. Teriberka was once a major centre of coastal fishing, and the old schooners lived out their days right by the shore.

data.name: Place2Detail2
data.value: Today the blackened hulls are the most recognisable view of Teriberka — they appeared in “Leviathan” and dozens of documentaries. Come at low tide, when you can walk almost up to the ships.

data.name: Place3Detail1
data.value: Lake Maloye Batareyskoye spills over the edge of a rocky canyon and falls straight into the Barents Sea. It is one of the few places in the world where a waterfall meets the ocean.

data.name: Place3Detail2
data.value: The name comes from a WWII artillery battery that defended the entrance to the bay; its positions survive nearby. A trail across stony tundra leads to the waterfall — wear non-slip shoes.

data.name: Place4Detail1
data.value: From the clifftop viewpoints you look out at the open ocean: beyond the horizon, all the way to the Pole, there is only water and ice. In winter the sea does not freeze thanks to the warm Gulf Stream.

data.name: Place4Detail2
data.value: In spring and early summer you can spot whales and orcas from the shore, and kittiwakes nest on the cliffs. Bring a thermos: the wind at the edge of the continent almost never stops.

data.name: Place5Detail1
data.value: From September to April it is dark enough above the Arctic Circle to see the aurora. We track solar activity and cloud cover and take the group to spots free of light pollution — the odds of seeing the lights in one night of hunting are high.

data.name: Place5Detail2
data.value: The aurora is capricious: sometimes a faint green haze, sometimes the whole sky dancing in waves from horizon to horizon. Dress in layers — the hunt means several hours in the cold, with hot tea and a tripod.

data.name: Place6Detail1
data.value: The road to Teriberka runs through true Arctic tundra: hills, lakes, dwarf birches and carpets of reindeer moss. In summer the tundra blooms with cloudberries and fireweed; in winter it becomes an endless white desert.

data.name: Place6Detail2
data.value: Along the way we stop at panoramic points — from here the Kola Peninsula looks just like in films about the North. With luck, we will meet reindeer.
